b385e489a4:
The guide lists seven things for this objective: function calling, descriptions, error handling, harness dispatch, client versus server tools, approval patterns and tool-set construction.

This chapter follows one tool call all the way through. It starts at the definition you send, moves through the tool_use block the model returns, into your dispatcher, out to a backend, and back as a tool_result. At each stage it asks what can go wrong and which piece of code owns the fix.

Along the way it covers:

  • the pairing rules that produce 400 errors, and parallel calls;
  • descriptions that route correctly, with a before-and-after misrouting example;
  • input schema design and strict mode;
  • structured error payloads, and who retries what;
  • a full dispatcher with a registry, timeouts, idempotency and bounded concurrency;
  • Anthropic's server tools and the pause_turn stop reason;
  • approval tiers with a human in the loop;
  • how many tools one agent should see;
  • the tool_choice restrictions on the current models;
  • the same registry in Java.

The material overlaps CCAR-F task statements 2.1 to 2.3 (tool interface design, structured errors, tool distribution and tool_choice), so it serves both exams.
a2c393f452: Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 20 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/21-tool-implementation/. Run bash run_all.sh. Everything runs offline on the shared fake client. toolkit.py holds the schema checker, protocol checker, typed errors and the dispatcher. telco.py is the running example: a telecom care agent with five tools. Example 20 compiles and runs the Java registry when a JDK is present.
8ffd35abda: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 02 owns the agent loop as a whole; this chapter only zooms into the tool step. Chapter 05 owns the Messages API request shape. Chapter 18 owns structured output, the JSON Schema subset and using a tool as an extraction contract. Chapter 19 owns prompt injection through tool results. Chapter 20 owns hooks as a safety layer. Chapter 22 owns MCP server authoring. Chapter 23 owns the choice between custom tools, Skills, MCP servers and built-in tools.
a8a58f081b:
A tool is a contract (name, description, input schema) that the model reads and fills in; Claude never executes anything, it emits a tool_use block, your harness decides whether and how to run it, and the outcome goes back as a tool_result with the same id in the very next user message, flagged is_error when it failed.

Everything that has to be guaranteed (valid input, authorisation, approval, timeouts, at-most-once writes, a bounded number of calls) lives in the dispatcher, and everything that has to be chosen well (which tool, which arguments, what to do after an error) is steered by the text you give the model: descriptions, schemas, enums and error messages.
dfcf65ad7f:
At 4.4% of 53 items, 8.1 is worth two or three direct questions. It is the largest objective in Domain 8. It also sits underneath every agent question on the exam, since an agent is a loop around tool calls.

The wrong options in tool questions follow a few patterns. They're worth knowing before you read the details:

  • a prompt instruction offered as the fix for something that needs code ("tell the model never to call delete");
  • a bigger model offered as the fix for a description problem;
  • a uniform error string that hides what went wrong;
  • a retry of something that cannot succeed;
  • a forced tool_choice on a model that rejects it;
  • one agent given every tool in the company.

The right option usually moves a guarantee into the harness. Or it puts the information the model needs into the description, the schema or the error payload.
37e5da4073: Tool calling is remote procedure call with an unusual caller. The lineage is worth knowing. Most of the engineering advice in this chapter is old advice applied to a new kind of client, and the exam's distractors are often ideas that made sense for older callers.
be0a2df05f: RPC and interface definitions. Sun RPC (1984), and later CORBA IDL, SOAP with WSDL (2000) and gRPC with Protocol Buffers (2015), all separate an interface description from its implementation. A client is generated from the description and never sees the server code. Tool definitions play the same role. The model sees the name, the description and the JSON Schema of the input. It never sees the function body.
410b689705: OpenAPI. Swagger (2011, OpenAPI from 2016) described REST endpoints with JSON Schema bodies and a free-text description per operation. For human client developers, the description was documentation. For a language model choosing among tools, it is the main input to the decision. That shift is why tool descriptions get a whole section here.
40ec0ea1cf:
Language models learn to act. The ReAct paper (Yao et al., 2022) showed a model interleaving reasoning with actions such as "Search[...]", which the harness parsed out of plain text. Toolformer (2023) trained a model to insert API calls into its own output.

Plain-text parsing was fragile, so providers moved the structure into the API. OpenAI function calling came first (June 2023), then Anthropic tool use (beta in 2024). The model now returns a typed tool_use block instead of text you have to parse.

Between 2024 and 2026 more followed: parallel tool calls, strict schema-constrained tool inputs, server-side tools that Anthropic runs itself (web search, code execution, web fetch), and tool search for very large tool sets.
b8b48b3643: Standardised tool servers. The Model Context Protocol (November 2024) made "a process that exposes tools" a reusable component. The same tools can now serve Claude Code, Claude Desktop and your own agents (chapter 22). MCP changes how tools are packaged and discovered. It does not change the cycle in this chapter. A tool from an MCP server still reaches the model as a name, description and schema, and its result still goes back as a tool result.
2e41c1461f:
Claude is a next-token predictor (chapter 13). When you pass tools, the API renders your tool definitions into a hidden system prompt. That prompt tells the model which tools exist and how to call them. The model has been trained to emit a call in a particular structured form when it decides a tool would help.

The API parses that output into a tool_use content block with three fields:

  • an id generated by the API (for example toolu_01A09q90qw90lq917835lq9);
  • the tool name;
  • an input object.

Generation then stops with stop_reason: "tool_use". Nothing has run. Your program now holds a request to run a function. It can run it, refuse it, ask a human, or run something else and report that.
c709e7334c: The model knows only what you wrote. It chooses tools by reading the name, the description and the schema. These are input tokens on every request of the loop, not a one-time registration. The docs publish the size of the hidden tool-use system prompt per model. For Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 it is 286 tokens with tool_choice auto or none, and 406 with any or tool, on top of your own definitions. Ten well-described tools at 200 tokens each add about 2,000 input tokens to every call. That's one reason prompt caching (chapter 15) matters for agents.
5f5940d509: Your harness is the trust boundary. Execution happens in your code, so every guarantee must live there too. "Never credit more than $50" in the system prompt is a probability. "maximum": 50 checked by the dispatcher, plus a check in the billing service, is a guarantee. The model can also be manipulated by text it reads in tool results (chapter 19). That's another reason the decision to execute cannot rest on the model alone.
8211e2c604: The API is stateless. Every request carries the whole conversation (chapter 05). You have to send back the assistant message containing the tool_use block exactly as received, and put the matching tool_result in the next user message. If the pairing is broken, the API returns a 400 rather than guessing what you meant.
aeacfac1e8: The Java analogy that holds up best goes like this. Tool definitions are an OpenAPI document. The model is a client generated from it, picking operations by reading their descriptions. Your dispatcher is the controller plus the Spring Security filter chain plus the transaction boundary. You would never put authorisation rules in an OpenAPI description field and trust clients to obey them. The same reasoning applies here.
aec484a534: A client tool (one you execute) is a JSON object in the tools array of the request. Three fields are required and several are optional. The table lists what the define-tools page documents as of October 2026. The last three optional fields belong to newer features and are described in the tool reference, so check the docs before you rely on their exact behaviour.
76548fdd47:
Anthropic-defined tools look different. You send a type string with a version date and a name, with no description or schema, because the model was trained on that tool's interface.

  • {"type": "web_search_20260209", "name": "web_search"} is a server tool that Anthropic runs.
  • {"type": "bash_20250124", "name": "bash"} and {"type": "text_editor_20250728", "name": "str_replace_based_edit_tool"} are Anthropic-schema client tools. The interface is Anthropic's, but you execute the calls.

Section 16 covers the difference.
38c10a3b6a:
Two details in that definition are easy to miss. First, the description says what the tool does not do ("does not change the order"). That stops the model from calling it to cancel an order and then telling the customer the order is cancelled. Second, the parameter has its own description with an example value. That's the cheapest way to get the format right.

Example 01_tool_definitions.py builds the running example's five tools. It checks the name rule, the object-typed schema and a minimum description length.
be23e7ed09:
Read the trace for what it implies about your loop code.

  • The assistant turn you append is the complete content array, text block included. Dropping the text, or re-creating the tool block from a parsed copy, can lose fields. With extended thinking it also loses the thinking blocks the API expects to see again.
  • The tools array is sent on every request, because the model has no memory of the previous call.
  • The result's content is a string here, but it can also be a list of text, image, document or search_result blocks. So a tool that renders a coverage map can return an image the model will look at.
  • The loop ends on stop_reason, not on what the text says (chapter 02).
144bb72e56: The tool_result content field is optional. An empty result (no content key) is legal. It means the tool ran and had nothing to say, for example a write that returns no body. Still, prefer returning a short confirmation such as {"ok": true, "ticket_id": "T-88123"}. The model reasons better when it can see the identifier it just created, and it can quote it to the user.
7250b3274a: The API reconstructs the conversation from what you send, so it validates the tool part of the transcript strictly. The rules below are quoted or paraphrased from the handle-tool-calls and parallel-tool-use pages. They cause most "my agent works for one call and fails on the second" bugs.
5816754691: Every tool_use gets a tool_result with the same tool_use_id. If the assistant turn has three calls, the next user message has three results. A call you decided not to run still gets a result, with is_error: true and a short reason ("skipped: earlier step failed"). The parallel-tool-use page says this explicitly.
7d0ce8ad48: Results come first in that message. "In the user message containing tool results, the tool_result blocks must come FIRST in the content array. Any text must come AFTER all tool results." A text block before a result is a 400. Text after the results is fine for client tools.
3a9a4aee89: All results of one turn go in one message. Splitting parallel results into several user messages is wrong twice. The transcript breaks rule 2 for the later results. And the docs warn that incorrect formatting "teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls".
32356a33d6: The order of results inside the message is free. They are matched by id, not by position. A dispatcher that finishes calls out of order can return them in any order. Returning them in request order is still the better habit, because it makes logs and tests deterministic.
ae1b196a55:
The error message to recognise is "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after". When you see it, look for one of three causes:

  • A result is missing. Often it's a call that raised an exception before the code built its result.
  • Text was put before the results.
  • Something was appended between the assistant turn and the results. A common one is a guardrail that appends a warning message.

Example 04_protocol_rules.py encodes the rules as a test table with eight transcript fragments. It includes the case that surprises people: an error result is still a valid result.
6cbf3eb55c: Parallel tool use is on by default. Claude 4 and later models use it when a request benefits from several independent calls. "Check account A-1001 and order ORD-7731" usually produces one assistant turn with two tool_use blocks. The API does not prescribe the execution order. You may run the calls concurrently, sequentially, or in a mix, and you return all results in one user message.
ad6237db31:
To limit it, set disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside tool_choice. It is not a top-level parameter. With auto it means at most one tool call per response (Claude may still answer in text without calling a tool). With any or tool it means exactly one. But those two values are rejected on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (section 18), so on the current default models the flag goes with auto.

The reasons to turn parallel calls off are narrow: tools with hidden ordering dependencies you cannot express, a backend that cannot take concurrent requests from one session, or a UI that shows one action at a time for approval. Turning it off to "make the agent safer" is usually the wrong fix. The dispatcher can serialise writes while still running reads in parallel (section 14).
215e32ca81:
When you want more parallelism, the docs list a few levers:

  • a system prompt section that asks for independent operations to be issued together (the docs give a <use_parallel_tool_calls> block);
  • correctly formatted results in history;
  • a metric, average tool calls per tool-calling message, which should be above 1.0 if parallel calls are working.

They also suggest telling the model to "only batch tool calls that are independent of each other". That matters when the second call needs the first call's output. The docs note that Fable 5.1 may issue fewer parallel calls in long agent loops, and point to a batching instruction in its prompting guide.
4302c00a18:
Parallel calls change what your dispatcher must guarantee. Say two calls in one turn both write to the same account. Run them concurrently and they can interleave in a way no sequential reading of the transcript would predict. The safe default:

  • reads run concurrently, with a bound;
  • writes run one at a time, in the order the model emitted them;
  • results go back with the right ids, whatever the finishing order.

Example 03_parallel_calls.py shows the broken split-message transcript next to the fixed one. Example 12_concurrency.py measures three 0.1 second reads finishing in about 0.1 seconds, and three writes applied in emitted order.
c4bd1ccc53:
When the model sees a request and a list of tools, it has to decide whether any tool helps, and which one. The only evidence it has is the text of the definitions and the conversation. If two descriptions say much the same thing, the decision becomes a guess weighted by small wording differences. If a description is one vague line, the model fills the gaps from the name and from what tools like that usually do.

Anthropic's guidance is blunt. Detailed descriptions are "by far the most important factor in tool performance". Aim for at least three or four sentences. Include what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and caveats such as what the tool does not return.
525eea698a: A care team ships an agent with three tools. Reviewers notice that questions like "is account A-1002 active?" sometimes call search, which returns help articles. The agent then explains how to check account status in the app instead of answering. The definitions were these:
98173e46f9:
Every description contains "information". Two contain "customer", one contains "status". Nothing says which data source each one reads, what identifiers they take, or which questions they are not for. A model choosing between them is choosing between synonyms.

The fix is not a bigger model, or a sentence in the system prompt ("prefer get_info for status questions"). The fix is to make the definitions distinct. Rename them, and rewrite the descriptions so that each owns a clear slice of the requests.
03b580f06f:
Example 05_description_routing.py makes the effect measurable. A deliberately crude selector (word overlap between the request and each definition) stands in for the model. With the vague set, all four test requests tie or score zero, so the choice is a coin flip. With the rewritten set, all four route correctly.

A real model reads far better than a word counter. But it fails the same way when descriptions overlap, and the remedy is the same. In production you measure this with a routing eval: a labelled set of requests with the expected tool, run on every change to a description (chapter 04 and chapter 12).
fbee93d3eb:
Three related levers sit next to the description.

Names carry weight because the model reads them first. get_info and lookup are names of mechanisms; orders_get_status is a name of a capability. The docs recommend namespacing by service.

The system prompt can undo a good description. If it says "always search the knowledge base first", the model will call the search tool for account questions. So when a tool misroutes, check the system prompt's keywords as well as the description (CCAR-F 2.1 names this explicitly).

Tool results teach too. A tool that returns a helpful "not_found; use billing_get_account for account ids" error corrects a misroute on the next step. That's cheaper than an extra paragraph in every request.
16839f90ea: One trap in descriptions: asking for the model's chain of thought as a parameter. The define-tools page warns that a parameter requesting step-by-step reasoning may trigger a refusal of category reasoning_extraction. Ask for an explanation or supporting evidence instead (a justification field, a quoted_evidence field). That's also more useful to a reviewer.
5aa7845217:
The input schema does two jobs. It tells the model how to fill the arguments. And it is the first check your dispatcher runs on what comes back.

A loose schema (every field a free string, nothing required) leaves room for trouble. The model can put "about twenty dollars" in an amount, a customer's name where an account id belongs, or an invented reason code. The damage then happens inside the tool, where it is harder to explain. A tight schema rejects those inputs at the boundary, with a message the model can act on.
d505fccce5: Example 06_schema_design.py feeds seven inputs a model might produce to a loose and a tight version of apply_credit. The loose schema accepts all seven. That includes a name where the account id should be, an amount of 500 and an extra waive_fees flag. The tight schema accepts only the correct one. For each of the others it returns a specific message, such as $.amount: 500 > maximum 50 or $: unexpected field 'waive_fees', which the model can use to correct itself.
240f96030b:
Two design choices need judgement.

Enums versus free text. An enum is right when the set is closed and owned by you (reason codes, plan tiers). Free text is right when the value comes from the user and is open (a search query, a note to a ticket). If a closed set occasionally needs an escape hatch, add other plus a detail field and count how often it is used. Don't let the model invent values. Chapter 18 uses the same pattern for extraction.

One tool with an action parameter versus several tools. The define-tools page suggests consolidating related operations into fewer tools with an action parameter, which keeps the tool list short. The cost is a schema whose valid fields depend on the action. That's harder to validate and harder for the model to fill.

A reasonable rule: consolidate operations that share arguments and risk (list, get and search on tickets). Keep separate any operation with a different approval tier (closing a ticket), so the approval policy can be attached to the tool name.
633cad33eb:
Without strict mode, Claude's tool inputs follow the schema almost always. The define-tools page says that when an input is invalid or missing parameters, Claude will usually retry two or three times with corrections after it sees your error. But "almost always" is not good enough when a malformed input reaches a system of record or breaks a typed client.

Setting "strict": true on a tool definition turns on grammar-constrained decoding for that tool's input. It's the same mechanism as JSON outputs (chapter 18). The schema is compiled into a grammar, and tokens that would leave it are masked. The strict-tool-use page states two guarantees: the input strictly follows the input_schema, and the tool name is always valid (one of the provided tools or server tools).
b8d930baa5:
What strict mode does not do follows from the mechanism.

It constrains form. A strict account_id with a pattern will match the pattern, but it may be the wrong account.

It only enforces the parts of JSON Schema the grammar compiler supports. Chapter 18 lists the subset. The point that matters for tools is that some constraints, such as numeric ranges and string length bounds, are not enforced by decoding. Your validator must still check them. The documented pattern closes every object with additionalProperties: false.

Compiled grammars are cached for up to 24 hours from last use, and the first request with a new schema pays compile latency. The docs warn not to put PHI in property names, enum values, const values or patterns, because schema caching does not get the same protections as message content. Chapter 18 gives the per-request limits on strict tools, optional parameters and union types. Check the docs for the current numbers before you design a large strict tool set.
06a8ce2bd5: Strict mode matters more on the current models than before, because of a restriction on tool_choice. On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, forcing a tool with any or tool returns a 400. The docs' recommended replacement is auto with strict: true for schema-valid inputs, or structured outputs when you want a fixed JSON response shape. On models that still accept forced tool use (Haiku 5.5, for example), combining any with strict tools guarantees two things: a tool is called, and its input is valid.
203e123447:
Example 07_strict_mode.py lints the running example and then shows the consequence concretely. A strictly decoded apply_credit input with "amount": 75.0 is a perfectly valid number. Only the dispatcher's own check against maximum: 50 catches it.

The general rule for the exam: strict mode moves shape errors to zero. Every semantic check stays in your code: ranges your compiler ignores, ownership, existence, policy.
fe5158af44:
Tools fail. The backend times out. The input names an order that does not exist. The caller is not allowed to see the account. The business rule forbids the action.

The worst responses to a failure are the two extremes. Raising an exception out of the loop kills the conversation and throws away everything the agent had learned. Returning a cheerful empty success ("[]" or "done") makes the model believe something false and tell the user.

The protocol has a specific place for failure: the same tool_result block, with is_error: true and content that explains what went wrong.
455b4856f3: The docs ask for instructive messages. Instead of "failed", say what went wrong and what Claude should try next, for example "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds." For anything beyond a toy, make the content structured, so the model and your logs can both read it. The payload used throughout the companion code has four fields that cover nearly every case:
260b8df0ea:
Why categories and a retryable flag, instead of a good sentence? Because the model has to choose between very different next actions: fix the input, ask the user, apologise, try later, escalate. A uniform "Error: operation failed" gives it nothing to decide with.

The structured fields also feed your own systems. A dashboard of error categories per tool shows when a description is causing validation errors, or when a backend is flaking. CCAR-F 2.2 uses the names errorCategory and isRetryable for the same idea in MCP results. The field names are yours to choose. The separation is what matters.
f90718bee5:
Two distinctions come up again and again in exam scenarios.

Access failure versus valid empty result. A search that ran and found no outages succeeded, and should return {"incidents": []} without is_error. A search that could not reach the outage database failed, and must say so. Collapse the two and the model will tell a customer "there is no outage in your area" when in fact the system did not know.

Customer-safe versus internal detail. The model reads the error content and may repeat it to the user. So it should carry a safe explanation and an internal error id for your logs. Never a stack trace, SQL or a column name. The companion dispatcher maps any unexpected exception to an internal error with a short hash id. Test test_tool_bug_does_not_leak_stack in example 19 checks that the exception text does not appear in the result.
965a870c9b: Example 08_error_payloads.py sends five failing calls through the dispatcher: not found, validation, business rule, policy deny, unknown tool. It prints the category, retryable flag and hint for each. Then it contrasts a uniform error with a valid empty result.
e603a4d514:
Retrying is a decision with two possible owners, and putting it in the wrong place is a common design error.

The harness should retry what the model cannot influence, and can only make worse by thinking about: a 503, a dropped connection, a rate limit with a known wait. The model should handle what needs judgement or a changed input: a validation error it can fix, a not-found it should take back to the user, a rule it should explain.

A useful test is whether a retry with the same input could succeed. If yes, and the failure is infrastructural, the harness retries with bounded exponential backoff. The model only hears about it if the retries run out. If no, the model gets the error once and decides what to do.
3fb26c4c9c: Writes need extra care. A timeout on a write does not tell you whether the write happened. The request may have been applied and the response lost. Blindly repeating it can double-charge a customer. You have two options: an idempotency key the backend honours (section 14), or a status check before any repeat. And the error the model sees should say "may have completed; check before repeating", not "failed".
977d938f36:
The model's own retry behaviour needs a bound too. If a tool keeps failing validation because the description is wrong, the model may call it again and again with small variations. Two things stop that: the loop's tool-call budget (example 17) and a per-tool consecutive-error counter. When the counter trips, return an error that says "stop calling this tool; tell the user you cannot complete this step". Record the event for whoever owns the description.

Example 09_retry_policy.py shows a transient failure retried invisibly by the harness, and a not-found sent straight to the model. It also prints the ownership table.
e5e803678c: The dispatcher is the code between the model's tool_use blocks and your functions. In a demo it is a dictionary lookup. In production it is where every non-negotiable property of the agent is enforced. It deserves the same design care as an API gateway. The companion toolkit.Dispatcher runs these checks for each call, in this order, and every failure becomes a typed error result for the same id:
2dc3f92560: Known tool. Look the name up in the registry. Unknown names can happen without strict mode, or after you remove a tool mid-conversation. They return not_found with the list of valid names as a hint.
bb2e76e761: Allowed for this caller. An allow-list per agent or role: a billing subagent may not call network tools. This is least privilege at the tool level. It backs up the cleaner option of not sending the definition at all.
004feebb1a: Schema. Validate input against input_schema even if the tool is strict. Strict decoding leaves some constraints unenforced, and definitions and code drift.
96dde08308: Wrap the return value as a result, or the exception as a structured error. Log the call with id, tool, outcome and latency.
61270eee3e: The registry keeps three things together that drift apart when they live in different files: the definition the model sees, the function that runs, and the operational metadata (tier, read-only, timeout, idempotency key). You generate the tools array from the registry. So a tool cannot be advertised without an implementation, or implemented without a tier. The registry also gives you one place to derive subsets: reg.definitions(names=ROLE_TOOLS["billing"]) for a scoped subagent.
bcf7453d17:
Timeouts are per tool, because a catalogue lookup and a provisioning call have different normal latencies. Without them, one hung backend holds the whole loop, and the user sees nothing. The dispatcher wraps each call in asyncio.wait_for and turns expiry into a timeout error result.

Example 10_timeouts.py shows a 0.5 second backend cut off at 0.2 seconds, while a fast call in the same turn still returns normally. It also documents a Python detail that bites in production. A synchronous function running in a worker thread cannot be killed. The thread keeps running after the timeout, and the interpreter waits for it at exit. Real cancellation needs async tool code, or a timeout on the HTTP client inside the tool. The dispatcher's timeout bounds what the model waits for, not what the backend does.
7597d82050:
The loop has budgets of its own on top of per-call timeouts: a maximum number of iterations, a maximum number of tool calls, and often a wall-clock deadline and a token budget. These are safety nets, not the stopping rule. The stopping rule is stop_reason (chapter 02). When a budget trips, the agent should end with a clear message and a log entry, not a stack trace.

Example 17_agent_loop_full.py combines the dispatcher with a loop that handles every stop reason. That includes a max_tokens stop with a truncated tool_use block. The docs' advice there: retry with a higher max_tokens, and never execute a partial call.
66d90df713:
Models repeat calls for ordinary reasons. A write timed out and the model tries again. Context compaction removed the earlier result, so the model does not know the credit was applied. The customer asked twice. A subagent and the coordinator both decided to act.

For reads, repetition costs tokens. For writes, it costs money or worse. The fix is the one you use for payment APIs: an idempotency key derived from the business meaning of the request, checked before execution, with the stored result returned for a repeat.
1437d5cbdf:
The key must be a business key. A repeated call from the model carries a new tool_use id every time, so keying on the id deduplicates nothing. Example 11_idempotency.py shows exactly that failure next to the fix.

For apply_credit the business key is order id plus reason: one credit per order per reason, whatever amount the model proposes the second time. Choose the key with the business owner, because it encodes a policy. Is a second credit for the same order but a different reason allowed? Here, yes.

Many payment and provisioning APIs support idempotency keys natively. Where they do, pass the same key through. Then a retry after a timeout is safe end to end, not just inside your process.
35ca120145:
Concurrency inside one turn follows from parallel calls (section 07). The companion dispatcher runs every call of a turn through asyncio.gather. A semaphore bounds concurrent execution (max_parallel, your back-pressure knob toward fragile backends). Writes sit behind a lock, so they run one at a time in the order the model emitted them. Reads do not need the lock. Results are returned in request order. Example 12_concurrency.py measures all three properties.

Across turns and across sessions, concurrency is a backend problem. Two agent sessions for the same customer can still race. You solve that the usual way, with optimistic locking or a version check in the service, not in the agent.
4ccf076c9c: Idempotency storage needs a lifetime. An in-memory dictionary is enough for one conversation in a demo. Production needs a store that survives restarts and is shared between replicas, with an expiry that covers the realistic retry window (minutes to a day, depending on the operation). A database unique constraint on the business key is often the simplest correct implementation.
9b01236c7a:
Every tool result becomes input tokens on every later request of the loop. Picture a tool that returns a 60-row raw dump with an internal routing blob per row. It can cost more tokens than the rest of the conversation. It can push important instructions out of the model's attention. And it can leak fields the model should not see.

The define-tools guidance is to return only high-signal information, using stable identifiers such as slugs or ids. In practice that means four habits:
d69b35d44a: Silent truncation is the bug to look for. If a tool returns the first 10 of 60 tickets with no indication, the model will say "there are 10 open tickets in 07302". Nothing downstream will catch it. Example 18_result_shaping.py compares a raw dump (about 9,000 tokens by the rough chars/4 estimate) with a shaped first page (about 300). It asserts that the shaped version reports truncated: true.
f04e4a8ba0:
Large or binary results have better homes than the text of a tool result.

  • An image (a coverage map) can go back as an image block inside the tool result content.
  • A long document can go back as a document block, or stay outside the conversation and be referred to by id.
  • For bulk data the model needs to compute over, programmatic tool calling (section 16) lets code in the sandbox call your tool and reduce the data before anything reaches the model's context.

Context management in long loops (clearing old tool results, compaction) is chapter 16.
83a0e65a8a:
The tool-use overview draws the line by where the code runs.

Client tools run in your application. That means every tool you define yourself, plus Anthropic-schema tools such as bash, text_editor and memory. Anthropic defines their interface and the model was trained on it, but you execute them. For client tools the model stops with stop_reason: "tool_use" and waits for your tool_result.

Server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure. You declare them with a versioned type and a name, and the API executes the call inside the same request. The response already contains both the call (server_tool_use) and its result block (for example web_search_tool_result). You write no handler and send no result.
36757453ef:
The versions in that table change several times a year, and the exam is unlikely to ask for a date suffix. What it will ask about is the distinction: which side executes, who pays, and what your loop must handle. Server tools such as web search carry a usage charge on top of tokens; check the pricing page.

Use a server tool when Anthropic's implementation is what you need and the data is public or provided in the request (current web information, sandboxed computation over an uploaded file). Use a client tool when the call needs your credentials, your network, your data, or your approval step. That covers every system of record in an enterprise.
ac43c69a3a:
Server tools add two cases to the loop.

The first is pause_turn. The server-side sampling loop has an iteration limit (10 by default, per the stop-reasons page). When it is reached, the response stops with pause_turn, possibly with a server_tool_use block that has no result yet. You continue by appending the assistant content unchanged and sending the request again, and the server resumes. A loop that treats every non-tool_use stop as the end will return a half-finished answer.

The second is mixed turns. If Claude calls a server tool and a client tool in the same parallel group, the response comes back with stop_reason: "tool_use", and the server tool has not run yet. Three rules apply:

  • You return tool_result blocks for the client calls.
  • The user message must contain only those results. Text after them ends the turn and produces a 400 naming the unresolved server tool.
  • You must keep the same tools array, including the server tool, or the request fails.

The API then runs the deferred server call and continues. There is no flag for this state. You detect it by checking whether each server_tool_use id has a matching result block. Example 14_server_tools.py scripts both cases.
94b4e07d20:
Programmatic tool calling blurs the line in a useful way. With a code execution version from _20260120 on, a client tool can set allowed_callers to include the code execution tool. Code running in the sandbox can then call it. Omitting "direct" means the model can only call the tool from code.

The tool still runs in your application; the tool_use block carries a caller field saying it came from code. But the model can write a loop that calls query_database fifty times and summarises the rows, so the fifty raw results never enter its context. It's the right pattern when a task needs many similar calls whose individual results don't matter to the reasoning. The exact semantics are new, so check the docs before building on them.
ee47c9371e:
Some tool calls should not run just because the model asked. The issue isn't whether the model is trustworthy in general. It's that a model's choice is probabilistic. It can be steered by text in tool results (chapter 19). And it is made without the accountability your business attaches to certain actions.

Approval patterns put a decision point between the proposal and the execution, sized to the risk of the action. The common shape is three tiers, assigned per tool (and sometimes per call):
9d96838507:
Three design points decide whether the pattern works.

Enforce in code, not the prompt. "Ask the user before applying credits" in the system prompt will usually be followed. But the exam's answer for anything with money or data loss is a programmatic gate. The tier lives in the registry, and the dispatcher checks it before execution (section 13). A model that skips the question still cannot apply the credit.

Least privilege first. A deny-tier tool that the agent never sees cannot be called, cannot be talked into by injected text, and costs no tokens. The deny tier in the dispatcher is a backstop for configuration mistakes, not the main control. Example 13_approval_tiers.py asserts that close_account is absent from the definitions the model receives.

Tiers can depend on arguments. A credit of $5 may be auto, $25 confirm, $500 deny. Put the rule in a policy function that sees the validated input. Then the threshold is one line of code your risk owner can review.
ddae001e89:
How the approval reaches a human depends on the product.

In a chat UI, the dispatcher pauses the loop. The UI shows the proposed action with its arguments in plain words ("Apply a $20.00 credit to account A-1001 for late delivery of ORD-7731"). The human's decision becomes either the real result or an approval_denied error.

In a back-office workflow, the approval may take hours. Persist the conversation and the pending tool_use block, return control, and resume the loop when the decision arrives. The pairing rules still apply, so the eventual next user message must contain the result for that id.

Show the human the validated arguments, not the model's prose about them. The prose and the arguments can disagree.
274a83a26a:
When the human declines, the model must not route around the decision. No trying a different tool with the same effect. No splitting a $45 credit into two $22.50 credits. Three things back this up: the error message says so explicitly, the tier applies to every tool with that effect, and argument-dependent policies look at the cumulative effect (sum of credits per account per day) rather than each call alone.

The same idea appears as permission modes and allow/deny rules in Claude Code and the Agent SDK (chapters 11, 20 and 23). There a PreToolUse hook or a canUseTool-style callback plays the dispatcher's approval role. The concept on the exam is the same.
9835a7c2d4:
Which tools an agent sees is a design decision with measurable effects. Every definition costs input tokens on every call. More importantly, every extra tool is another candidate in each routing decision. The chance of picking a wrong but plausible tool grows with the number of near neighbours.

CCAR-F 2.3 states the pattern the exam tests. An agent with 18 tools selects less reliably than one with four or five focused tools. And agents given tools outside their specialty tend to misuse them: a synthesis agent with a web search tool starts searching instead of synthesising.

There is no official maximum. The useful rule is that each agent gets the tools its role needs, and nothing that duplicates another tool's slice.
bc150e69aa: Scope by role. A coordinator that delegates does not need the billing write tools. The billing subagent does not need network diagnostics. Give a subagent a small cross-role tool only when the round trip through the coordinator is the common case. A verify_fact tool for a synthesis agent is the CCAR-F example.
765991f820: Remove overlap. Two tools whose descriptions overlap heavily will misroute. Merge them, or rewrite them so each names the other as the alternative (section 08). Example 16_toolset_lint.py flags pairs with high description overlap, short descriptions and too many tools. It can run in CI on the definitions you ship.
307eedd341: Split generic tools. A single run_sql or call_api tool is easy to write and hard to use correctly. The model has to know your schema, and the approval tier cannot tell a read from a delete. Purpose-specific tools (orders_get_status, tickets_close) carry their own descriptions, schemas and tiers.
71d9bbdd63: For very large catalogues, defer. Mark rarely used tools defer_loading: true and include a tool search tool. The deferred definitions stay out of the initial prompt, and are expanded when the search returns a reference to them. Deferred tools are stripped before the prompt-cache key is computed, so adding one does not invalidate an existing cache entry. Check the docs for the toolset-specific rules.
27e71866f5:
tool_choice has four values:

  • auto: the model decides. This is the default when tools are present.
  • any: the model must call some tool.
  • tool with a name: the model must call that tool.
  • none: no tool calls. This is the default when no tools are passed.

When any or tool is used, the API prefills the assistant turn to force the call. So the model emits no text before the tool_use block, even if asked, and forcing a tool also skips thinking. Changing tool_choice between requests invalidates cached message blocks, though tool definitions and the system prompt stay cached.
bfb62dcb72:
So a pattern taught in older material, "force the extraction tool with tool_choice: {type: tool}", is a 400 on the default recommended model.

On Opus 5.5 you get the same reliability another way. Make the tool strict, leave tool_choice on auto with a clear instruction to use it, and handle the no-call case in code. Or, if the tool exists only to shape output, drop the tool and use JSON outputs (chapter 18). Prompting still influences which tool auto picks on these models.

Example 15_tool_choice_rules.py encodes the restrictions as a request validator you can put in front of your client. It even catches the misplaced top-level disable_parallel_tool_use flag.
53b8e2ca52:
Everything in sections 13 and 14 maps onto patterns a Spring architect already uses:

  • The registry is a Map<String, ToolHandler> built from beans.
  • The definition is generated from an annotated record or a JSON Schema generator.
  • Validation is Bean Validation on the input record, plus a schema validator.
  • The tier is an annotation read by an aspect or by the dispatcher.
  • Timeouts come from a bounded executor or Resilience4j's TimeLimiter.
  • Transient retries are Resilience4j Retry with exponential backoff.
  • Idempotency is a unique constraint on a business key in the database.

The structure below is plain Java, so it compiles without dependencies (companion java/ToolRegistryDemo.java, run by example 20). In a Spring Boot service, each ToolSpec would be a @Component implementing a ToolHandler interface, and the dispatcher would be injected with List<ToolHandler>.
92c1d31d51:
Two Java-specific notes.

The Anthropic Java SDK models tool_use and tool_result as typed blocks, so the dispatcher's signature uses the SDK types. The names above follow the SDK's naming pattern; check the SDK reference for the exact classes in your version.

Generating the input schema from a record with a JSON Schema generator is convenient, but review the output. Generators tend to produce open objects, miss enum descriptions and mark everything optional. Those are exactly the properties sections 09 and 10 ask you to control.

Spring AI also offers a tool abstraction (@Tool-annotated methods). It handles registration and the protocol for you. The same design questions still apply: descriptions, tiers, idempotency, error payloads.
dcc0a0cc66:
This trace puts the pieces together on one conversation with the running example (companion telco.py, dispatcher from toolkit.py). The customer writes: "My order ORD-7732 still hasn't arrived and I want a credit. My account is A-1002."

The agent runs on Opus 5.5 with tool_choice left on auto. It has four advertised tools (close_account is not sent), and a policy that auto-approves nothing that writes.
ffa872d7f7:
Three things in this trace are typical of what goes wrong without the patterns in this chapter.

  • Without step 4, the credit would have been applied to an order under fraud review. A sentence in the prompt saying "do not credit orders on hold" might have prevented it. It might not.
  • Without the structured error in step 5, the model would only know that "the operation failed". A common response to that is to try again.
  • Without the cumulative policy in step 7, a rephrased request with a different reason code would have reached the approver again. The approver might approve it in a hurry.

The model's behaviour in step 6 is not malicious. It is the model trying to satisfy the customer's explicit request. That is exactly why the guarantee has to be in code.
032ae143d3: The trace also shows what the model does well when the harness gives it good material. It called the two reads in parallel without being told. It chose the right tool for each identifier. And its final answer used the hold reason it had read to explain the situation in customer terms. Good descriptions, typed errors with hints and shaped results are what make that possible.
6d13e77b79: Tools have two audiences, and each needs its own tests. The dispatcher and the tool functions are ordinary code: unit tests, contract tests, failure injection. The definitions are an interface read by a model. They need routing evals that measure whether the model picks the right tool and fills the arguments correctly. Run them on every change to a description, a schema or the system prompt.
d5eb1005e3:
Routing evals are where description changes earn their keep. Keep a labelled set of a few hundred real requests per agent, each with the expected tool (or "no tool") and the key arguments. Run it on the real model for every change to definitions or the system prompt. Track accuracy per tool, not just overall, because a new tool usually steals traffic from one specific neighbour.

Example 19_dispatcher_tests.py holds eleven contract tests that run offline in under a second. Run it in CI the way you would run controller tests.
ba37ba23f7: Descriptions are the main input to tool selection, and these three are near-synonyms. Rewriting them, and renaming to capabilities such as billing_get_account and help_search_articles, removes the ambiguity at its source. B patches one symptom and leaves the overlap for every other phrasing. A treats a contract problem as a capability problem. D is keyword routing in code, which breaks on phrasing. And forced tool_choice returns a 400 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.
65e3d6a7bd: On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, both any and tool return 400. The documented replacements are strict tools with auto, or structured outputs for a fixed response shape. B fails the same way. D fails because prefill returns 400 on 4.6 and later models. A avoids the problem rather than solving it, and gives up the newer model.
8fb7dbfa4d: An access failure and a valid empty result are different facts, and they must look different to the model. B makes every genuine "no outage" answer wrong. C retries in the wrong place (the harness owns transient retries) and still ends with []. D leaks internals and does not tell the model what to do.
70231ddba9: Only code between proposal and execution can guarantee that a call does not run. Least privilege, meaning you don't advertise the tool to agents that should never use it, is the strongest version. A is probabilistic and can be overridden by injected text. C relies on an uncalibrated self-report (chapter 18). D limits concurrency, not authority.
e729af4358: In a mixed parallel group, the server tool is deferred until you return the client results. Text after the results ends the turn, and the API then fails on the unresolved server call. Dropping the server tool definition is itself a 400. The fix: results only, and the same tools array.
9f992aa6d5: Write a routing eval harness that can run against the real API with --live. It should use 20 labelled requests, report accuracy per tool, and diff against the previous run.
